articles.title: San Pedro Bay Ports Mark 20 Years of Landmark Clean Air Action Plan
articles.summary: Twenty years after adopting the landmark Clean Air Action Plan (CAAP), the ports of Long Beach and Los Angeles are advancing a new phase of clean air initiatives, building on two decades of dramatic reductions in air pollution while accelerating the transition to zero-emission operations. First adopted on Nov. 20,...
articles.body: San Pedro Bay Ports Mark 20 Years of Landmark Clean Air Action Plan in Port News 22/11/2026 Twenty years after adopting the landmark Clean Air Action Plan (CAAP), the ports of Long Beach and Los Angeles are advancing a new phase of clean air initiatives, building on two decades of dramatic reductions in air pollution while accelerating the transition to zero-emission operations. First adopted on Nov. 20, 2006, the CAAP established a coordinated strategy to reduce air pollution from ships, trucks, trains, cargo-handling equipment and harbor craft. Since 2005, combined port-related emissions of diesel particulate matter have fallen 90%, nitrogen oxides 70% and sulfur oxides 98%, even as the ports have handled growing volumes of international trade. “The Clean Air Action Plan is an amazing story of collaboration, innovation and persistence. Together, our two ports have made great strides in air quality and are committed to going to the next level – zero emissions,” said Steven Neal, President of the Long Beach Board of Harbor Commissioners. “As we celebrate 20 years of achievements, please understand that we are also planning even more clean air action for the years ahead.” “Twenty years ago, the Clean Air Action Plan fundamentally changed how we think about the relationship between our ports and the communities we serve,” said Los Angeles Harbor Commission President Beatrice Hsu. “We have demonstrated that a thriving global trade gateway and healthier communities can go hand in hand. Our responsibility now is to build on that progress, embrace innovation and ensure that future generations inherit a healthier, more sustainable harbor.” The CAAP has evolved considerably over the past 20 years, adapting to new technologies, regulatory requirements and environmental priorities. Today, the CAAP continues to guide both ports as they work to expand zero-emission operations, develop supporting infrastructure and establish additional commitments to reduce emissions. “What began here 20 years ago has transformed the San Pedro Bay ports complex and reverberated across our industry, all while we experience the busiest years in our history,” said Port of Long Beach CEO Dr. Noel Hacegaba. “Today, we’re forging Green Shipping Corridors with leading ports in Asia, developing Green Truck Corridors to Canada and Mexico and expanding our playbook of pioneering voluntary programs to drive emissions toward zero. We won’t stop until we cross that goal line.” “When we adopted the Clean Air Action Plan, we created a framework for sustained transformation of the port complex,” said Port of Los Angeles Executive Director Gene Seroka. “We’ve made enormous progress, but this was never meant to be a finish line. The CAAP has continued to evolve, and so have the technologies and strategies available to us. Now our focus is on getting more zero-emission equipment into service, building the infrastructure to support it and delivering the next round of emissions reductions.” Over the past two decades, the CAAP has produced measurable results and helped bring cleaner technologies into widespread use. Among its major accomplishments: Clean Truck Program: Launched in 2008, the program replaced thousands of older, higher-polluting trucks serving the ports and reduced truck-related air pollution by more than 90% in just over three years in advance of state regulations. Cleaner ships: Vessel speed reduction programs have achieved compliance rates exceeding 95% within 20 nautical miles of the harbor, while the widespread installation of shore power has allowed ships to shut down auxiliary engines while at berth. Technology Advancement Program: Since 2007, the ports have invested $61.3 million in total to support the development and demonstration of cleaner trucks, cargo-handling equipment and other technologies, helping move promising concepts toward commercial deployment. With funding from other agencies, a total of $445 million has been invested. Zero-emission equipment: Both ports have supported the introduction of battery-electric and hydrogen-powered trucks and cargo-handling equipment through demonstration projects, incentives and infrastructure investments. Coordinated environmental programs: The CAAP established a framework for joint planning, implementation and public reporting, bringing the ports, industry, government agencies and other stakeholders together around common air quality objectives. Originally developed with support from regional, state and federal air quality agencies, the CAAP was updated in 2010 and 2017 to incorporate new technologies, changing regulatory requirements and more ambitious emissions-reduction goals. The EPA has hailed the CAAP as a trailblazing effort and a national model for the rest of the country to follow. Building on 20 Years of Progress The next phase of the CAAP will focus heavily on moving zero-emission (ZE) technologies from demonstration projects to broader deployment across the San Pedro Bay ports complex. The 2017 CAAP update established goals of 100% ZE cargo-handling equipment drayage trucks. Reaching those goals will require more than replacing equipment. It will also depend on developing sufficient charging and fueling infrastructure, ensuring equipment can meet demanding port operating requirements, and addressing the substantial costs associated with the transition. The recently adopted Cooperative Agreement with the South Coast Air Quality Management District establishes a time-bound framework for development of ZE infrastructure. Both ports are now working with their terminal and utility partners to develop zero-emission infrastructure plans, with initial drafts expected May of next year. In addition, to support broader adoption of ZE equipment, the ports adopted “CAAP Plus” measures, which include new incentive programs and regional infrastructure investment. These measures were adopted in an addendum to the Cooperative Agreement. The ports are also pursuing groundbreaking initiatives that extend beyond equipment operating within the harbor. Work on cleaner marine fuels and Green Shipping Corridors is aimed at reducing emissions from oceangoing vessels and the international shipping routes that connect Southern California with trading partners around the world. These efforts build on an approach that has guided the CAAP since its adoption: setting environmental goals, working with industry and regulatory partners to develop practical solutions, and measuring results through annual emissions inventories and other public reporting. Source: Port of Long Beach 2026-11-22 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.title: Barclays warns of further equity weakness as hawkish Fed bets build
articles.summary: Equities could weaken further into year-end if Federal Reserve communication turns more hawkish or inflation data comes in hot, as investors question whether the central bank’s support has disappeared, according to Barclays. Strategists led by Emmanuel Cau said the “bigger challenge for equities is the perception...
articles.body: Barclays warns of further equity weakness as hawkish Fed bets build in Stock News 22/11/2026 Equities could weaken further into year-end if Federal Reserve communication turns more hawkish or inflation data comes in hot, as investors question whether the central bank’s support has disappeared, according to Barclays. Strategists led by Emmanuel Cau said the “bigger challenge for equities is the perception that the Fed put has disappeared,” beyond recent volatility in AI-linked stocks. Strong growth and sticky inflation have driven a sharp repricing of rate expectations, they said. That has tightened financial conditions, strengthened the dollar, drained excess liquidity and lowered valuations. Barclays compared the situation with December 2018, when equities fell about 20% before the Fed pivoted to a more dovish stance and stocks rallied sharply in early 2019. Markets now fully price a December rate increase, and comments by Fed Governor Christopher Waller have fueled some speculation of a 50 basis point move. Barclays economists disagree, arguing such a step would signal panic and imply that October’s pause was a mistake. Markets still price about three hikes over the coming year, which the strategists said is at odds with the moves in equities. “If the recent equity weakness reflects genuine concern that the AI investment cycle is fading, that should ultimately translate into weaker growth and less overheating pressure, reducing the need for the Fed to overtighten,” they wrote. A material AI slowdown and a much more hawkish Fed are therefore difficult to sustain indefinitely, they added. The December Fed meeting and the following CPI report are the key catalysts for risk appetite into year-end, the strategists said. A hotter print or more hawkish messaging would raise the risk of further weakness, while less hawkishness could calm nerves. “The end of the year is thus unlikely to provide much respite to investors,” they said. The strategists also noted that markets increasingly show “late-cycle vibes,” with IT outages and cyber incidents adding to fragile sentiment. They flagged a disconnect with fundamentals, citing positive surprises in U.S. retail sales and Germany’s ZEW survey, and continued positive earnings momentum. “Nvidia’s results reaffirmed that the capex cycle remains intact despite recent turbulence. Our house view remains that the AI hype may have peaked, but not the investment race,” the strategists said. They also stressed that late cycle “is not the same as end cycle,” and the recent risk-off move looks to be getting ahead of itself. Barclays continues to favor cyclical stocks exposed to the investment super-cycle. Source: Investing.com 2026-11-22 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.body: Asia week ahead: BoK rate decision, data from China, Taiwan, Japan in Stock News 22/11/2026 Korea: BOK expected to hike rates by 25bp The Bank of Korea is expected to raise its policy rate by 25bp to 3.25% on Wednesday, marking the third hike of the current tightening cycle. Inflation remains above target, with both headline and core CPI holding at 2.8% year-on-year in October, while robust semiconductor exports continue to underpin growth. At the same time, a moderation in household credit growth suggests earlier rate hikes are beginning to tighten financial conditions. China: Industrial profits recovery remains uneven China will release October industrial profits on Friday. While profits have generally recovered over 2026, the rebound remains uneven. Gains have been concentrated in AI- and electronics-related industries and upstream commodity producers, while automakers, construction-linked sectors, and many consumer-facing manufacturers continue to face significant pressure. Soft domestic demand is likely to keep these sectors under pressure in the October data. Taiwan: Technology supports industrial production growth Taiwan will release October industrial production data. We expect output growth to accelerate to 22.0% YoY, driven primarily by continued strength in the technology sector. Outside of tech, however, activity is likely to remain more subdued. A strong reading would reinforce expectations for solid economic growth in the fourth quarter. Japan: Tokyo inflation expected to strengthen Japan will release November Tokyo CPI data on Thursday. Consensus forecasts headline inflation to accelerate to 3.1% YoY from 2.8% in October, while core inflation is expected to rise to 2.9% YoY from 2.6%. A broadly in-line reading would suggest underlying price pressures remain firm and reinforce our expectations for a Bank of Japan rate hike in December. articles.title: ECB to expand currency swap lines, Lagarde says
articles.summary: The European Central Bank plans to make its currency swap lines with other countries more accessible to protect the euro area from external financial shocks and strengthen the euro’s global position, ECB President Christine Lagarde said. The ECB currently maintains swap lines only with major central banks including...
articles.body: ECB to expand currency swap lines, Lagarde says in World Economy News 22/11/2026 The European Central Bank plans to make its currency swap lines with other countries more accessible to protect the euro area from external financial shocks and strengthen the euro’s global position, ECB President Christine Lagarde said. The ECB currently maintains swap lines only with major central banks including the US Federal Reserve and the People’s Bank of China. These arrangements allow central banks to exchange their own currencies for euros during periods of financial market disruption. Lagarde’s remarks indicate these financial tools may eventually become available to a broader range of countries as the ECB works to increase international use of the euro and reduce the euro zone’s reliance on the US dollar for trade and investment. “We are working to keep our swap lines fit for purpose in a more fragmented world,” Lagarde told a conference. “They will be more accessible, too.” Policymakers worldwide have raised questions about the dollar’s long-term dominance given U.S. President Donald Trump’s unpredictable economic policy and the United States’ growing public debt. Lagarde said the main purpose of the swap lines is to limit the spread of financial stress from abroad, which indirectly helps the ECB manage borrowing costs in the euro area. She added that these central bank swaps increase foreign investors’ confidence in holding euros. “A reserve manager who knows that euro securities can be turned into euro liquidity without a fire sale has more reason to hold them in normal times,” Lagarde said. The ECB recently opened its EUREP facility, which permits foreign central banks to obtain euros against collateral denominated in the single currency. More than 30 countries have expressed interest in accessing the facility. Source: Investing.com 2026-11-22 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.title: Fed’s Paulson open to back-to-back rate hikes at steady pace
articles.summary: Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia President Anna Paulson said today she would consider consecutive interest-rate increases at upcoming policy meetings to address inflation, while emphasizing the need for a measured approach. “The direction of travel, in terms of where rates need to go, is really clear,” Paulson...
articles.body: Fed’s Paulson open to back-to-back rate hikes at steady pace in World Economy News 22/11/2026 Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia President Anna Paulson said today she would consider consecutive interest-rate increases at upcoming policy meetings to address inflation, while emphasizing the need for a measured approach. “The direction of travel, in terms of where rates need to go, is really clear,” Paulson said today in an interview with Bloomberg News in New York. “They need to be higher.” Paulson said she favored moving in a “deliberate way” to give households, businesses and banks more time to adjust. She did not commit to a specific schedule for rate increases. “I am not committed to every other meeting or every meeting,” she said. The Fed raised its benchmark rate by a quarter percentage point to a range of 3.75% to 4% in September, then held steady last month. Minutes from that meeting showed nearly all policymakers believed additional tightening would be needed in coming months. Multiple Fed officials have indicated support for another rate increase at the Dec. 8-9 meeting in Washington. Governor Christopher Waller said this week that policymakers should consider a half-point increase in December. Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack has advocated for small but successive increases. “I’m certainly open to considering that. I think that’s a very reasonable thing to have on the table,” Paulson said regarding the possibility of consecutive rate hikes. The Philadelphia Fed chief votes on monetary policy this year but not in 2027. Paulson said she is monitoring for signs of accelerating inflation pressures or higher risks from imbalances between supply and demand in the economy. A measured pace would allow the central bank time to respond to changing economic conditions, she said. “There are a lot of different ways that the economy could evolve from here, and so being able to not be too far ahead or too far behind, I think is helpful in having policy in a good place to respond if there’s a big change in the narrative,” she said. Investors expect rate increases in December and January, though the odds of the latter have declined amid sharp drops in equity markets driven by technology stocks. Paulson said the economy is doing “pretty well” as hiring has expanded and consumption has proven stronger than expected earlier this year. Taming elevated inflation is the “priority,” she said. “I’m focused on bringing inflation down in a way that balances the risks to both sides of the mandate. Clearly inflation is the priority, but there are risks on both sides,” she said, referring to the Fed’s goals for full employment and price stability. Inflation excluding food and energy items rose more than expected in October, driven by increases in grocery prices, rents and electricity. Policymakers will receive updated inflation numbers next week with the personal consumption expenditure price index for October. Paulson, a former research director at the Chicago Fed, said today there is no evidence that isolated cases of wage pressures are spreading broadly into the labor market. “At the same time, they are the kind of anecdotes that catch my ear because wage growth has been consistent with 2% inflation,” she said. “So anything that disrupts that I think is deserving of attention.” Source: Investing.com 2026-11-22 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

REUTERS/U.S. Navy/Handout SYDNEY, Nov 22 (Reuters) – Australian Defence Minister Richard Marles on Sunday criticized the United States Congressional Budget Office over a report that said the AUKUS pact would decrease the number of attack submarines available to the US Navy. “They are wrong,” Marles said, referring to the CBO, which said in the report this month that the sale of Virginia-class submarines to Australia could diminish the size of the navy’s attack submarine force through to 2060. AUKUS, Australia’s largest-ever defense project, will put US-commanded Virginia-class submarines in Australia from next year, involves selling several Virginia-class submarines to Australia from around 2030 and will have Britain and Australia build a new class of AUKUS nuclear-powered submarine. Marles was not worried about the report “ because AUKUS is very much happening ” and “the production rate in the United States is absolutely increasing,” he said in televised remarks. In October, Marles said Australia remained on track ?to acquire its first ?nuclear-powered subs from the US in the early 2030s. The CBO did not immediately respond to a request for comment outside regular business hours. Canberra has committed A$368 billion ($243 billion) over three decades to AUKUS, including billions of dollars in investment in British and US production bases. Formed in 2021, AUKUS is part of efforts to counter China’s growing influence in the Indo-Pacific. China has called the pact dangerous and warned it could spur a regional arms race. Finnish Border Guard/Handout via REUTERS HELSINKI, Nov 22 (Reuters) – A fire onboard a Russian cargo ship that was struck by drones in the Baltic Sea continued to burn through the night even as efforts were made to douse the flames, Finland’s coast guard said on Sunday. The Finnish military has said the strike on the Sparta II on Saturday was likely carried out by Ukraine and that the vessel later drifted into Finnish waters where it remains at anchor. The 16 crew members were evacuated onto a nearby Russian ship. Pictures and video released by the coast guard showed several vessels spraying the Sparta II with water cannons during the night in a bid to put out the flames and cool down containers stacked on its deck. Ukraine has sent waves of military drones towards Russia’s northwest coastal Leningrad region this year, including some that strayed into the airspace of nearby Baltic countries, leading to fears that the war was spilling onto NATO territory. The ship, bound for Russian exclave Kaliningrad, was damaged in international waters west of Russia’s Gogland island, Finland’s Defence Forces have said, corroborating an account by Russian officials. The risk of further attacks in the Gulf of Finland, a narrow arm of the Baltic Sea, cannot be ruled out, Estonian Navy Commander Ivo Vark told public broadcaster ERR on Sunday. Finland’s military said last week it had detected a strike on a Russian warship in the same area during Ukrainian drone attacks. The Sparta II is a 121-m (397-foot) Russian-flagged cargo vessel owned by Russian shipping company Oboronlogistika that left St Petersburg on Friday, according to LSEG data. The vessel is subject to US sanctions, according to the US Treasury Department. Oboronlogistika provides logistics services for the Russian Defence Ministry, according to the company’s website. articles.body: Cool Carriers has taken delivery of Snow Land, the third vessel in its seven-ship Snow-class newbuilding programme. Kitanihon Shipbuilding delivered the ice-class vessel in Japan on 12 November 2026. According to Cool Carriers, Snow Land is the world’s first specialised refrigerated cargo vessel equipped with a gate rudder. The Gate Rudder System replaces the conventional single rudder behind the propeller with two high-lift foil rudders positioned on either side of it. During voyages, water flowing across the rudder blades generates additional forward thrust, allowing the vessel to maintain speed while consuming less fuel. Each blade can also be controlled separately to improve manoeuvrability during berthing operations. Wärtsilä, a licensee of the technology, has reported fuel savings of up to 20% on vessels using the system. Kitanihon Shipbuilding said Snow Land’s overall design achieves a carbon dioxide intensity approximately 50% below the reference level for a vessel of its type and size. The calculation is based on the Energy Efficiency Design Index and operation using heavy fuel oil. Refrigerated cargo capacity Snow Land measures 162.5 metres in length and 25 metres in breadth, with a fully laden service speed of approximately 18 knots. The vessel provides 660,738 cubic feet, or 18,710 cubic metres, of refrigerated cargo capacity. Eight cooling zones allow fresh and frozen products to be transported at different temperatures ranging from -25°C to 15°C during the same voyage. Snow Land can also carry up to 168 forty-foot refrigerated containers on deck. The vessel follows sister ships Snow Flower and Snow Flake. Cool Carriers expects the remaining four Snow-class vessels to join its fleet over the next two years. “The Snow-class reflects our ongoing commitment to innovation and efficiency. It enables us to design new and exclusive itineraries, offer a higher standard of service and use next-generation environmental technologies that support our decarbonisation goals,” said Glenn Selling, Chief Operations Officer at Cool Carriers.

articles.body: Container traffic at the terminals managed by the Port Authority of València remains virtually stable, with the rolling twelve-month total of 5,628,895 TEUs up 0.15%. Rail traffic reached 258,910 TEUs, up 20.26 percent on 2025, further strengthening the role of rail in logistics linked to Valenciaport. Vehicle traffic handled as cargo has risen 9 percent year-on-year, including a 27% jump in October alone, when the automotive terminals at Sagunto and València handled 61,793 vehicles. From 1 January to 30 October, cargo traffic at the ports of València, Sagunto and Gandia totalled 65,931,152 tonnes, down 2.08 percent, while container traffic reached 4,718,532 TEUs, down 0.71 percent. In October alone, cargo traffic amounted to 6,681,689 tonnes, down 1.6%, and container traffic to 473,487 TEUs, up 1.1%. On a rolling twelve-month basis, the ports handled 78,664,787 tonnes, down 1.74%. Vessel calls were equally steady: 7,309 over the last twelve months against 7,310 in the previous period. Imports remain the main driver of activity. Full import containers have grown 10.79% since January to 959,880 TEUs, while full exports totalled 760,096 TEUs, a marginal decline of 0.04%. The sectors with the highest growth were vehicles and automotive parts (+10.12%), processed construction materials (+4.54%) and chemical products (+2.36%).

articles.body: The Port of Los Angeles has released a Draft Environmental Impact Report for a proposed Marine Oil Terminal and Wharf Improvements Project at Berths 148-151 in Wilmington, a terminal operated by Phillips 66. The report is intended to gather further feedback that will be incorporated into the Final Environmental Impact Report. Phillips 66 proposes to build a new berthing facility at Berths 150-151 that complies with the Marine Oil Terminal Engineering and Maintenance Standards. The existing wharf at Berths 148-149 would continue to serve as a marine oil terminal while the new facilities are under construction. Afterwards, its uses would be limited to non-terminal functions such as storing topside equipment and occasionally mooring harbour craft to reduce congestion in the channel. Landside facilities, including piping, vapour recovery systems, support systems and tankage, would be modified and upgraded to serve the new loading platform. The project considers up to 40 years of continued operation as a marine oil terminal at Berths 148-151, proposed through a new 20-year entitlement with two optional 10-year extensions. The environmental review began with an Initial Study and Notice of Preparation released in February 2023.

articles.summary: A Russian cargo ship linked to Moscow’s military logistics network caught fire after a drone strike in the Gulf of Finland on Saturday, drifting into Finnish territorial waters and triggering...
articles.body: Advertise Forum Jobs Subscribe Grab a Seat at the Captain’s Table Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe. Join the leading maritime news network Flames and thick smoke rise from the Russian-flagged cargo ship Sparta II in the Gulf of Finland on November 21, 2026, following a suspected drone attack. The vessel later drifted into Finnish territorial waters, prompting a response by Finnish authorities. A Russian cargo ship linked to Moscow’s military logistics network caught fire after a drone strike in the Gulf of Finland on Saturday, drifting into Finnish territorial waters and triggering an emergency maritime rescue operation. The Russian-flagged Sparta II , a sanctioned cargo vessel with a history of transporting military equipment, was struck in international waters west of Gogland Island, known in Finnish as Suursaari, according to Finland’s Ministry of Defence. Finnish military authorities detected the attack at approximately 8:40–8:50 a.m. local time, when the vessel was roughly 50 kilometers west of the island. The damaged ship subsequently lost maneuverability and drifted into Finnish territorial waters, where the Finnish Border Guard assumed responsibility for coordinating rescue operations. The incident took another turn shortly after midday when a Russian helicopter was suspected of entering Finnish airspace near Loviisa, reaching as far as 4.1 kilometers (2.5 miles) into Finnish territory. Finland’s Defence Minister Antti Häkkänen said the suspected airspace violation may have been connected to rescue or surveillance operations involving the damaged cargo ship. “The suspected airspace violation may be related to rescue or monitoring operations concerning the damaged cargo vessel in the Gulf of Finland,” Häkkänen said in a statement translated from Finnish. The Finnish Border Guard is investigating the incident, which occurred at approximately 12:34 p.m. local time. Fire Raises Fears of Explosions and Sinking The Sparta II remained ablaze Saturday afternoon, with Finnish authorities warning that the uncontrolled fire could lead to further explosions or even the loss of the vessel. The Finnish Border Guard said rescue vessels had reached the scene south of Loviisa, where authorities established a restricted area around the damaged ship. An official update issued at 2:58 p.m. local time said the crew had not been forced to abandon the vessel and that no environmental damage had been detected. Finnish authorities were preparing to assist with firefighting, evacuate personnel if necessary, and respond to any marine pollution. In a subsequent briefing reported by Yle, Finnish officials said the ship’s 16 crew members were evacuating into rescue craft. The vessel had anchored at approximately 3:45 p.m., and the anchor was holding. Russian rescue vessels were expected to arrive later Saturday. According to Finnish officials, Russia intended to tow Sparta II back into Russian waters once rescue operations were completed. The Finnish Border Guard emphasized that foreign vessels would require Finnish permission to participate in rescue operations within its area of responsibility. Sanctioned Vessel With Russian Military Connections The roll-on/roll-off Sparta II , IMO 9160994, is associated with Oboronlogistika, a Russian state-linked logistics company that provides maritime transportation services supporting the Russian Ministry of Defence. The vessel has previously been identified as part of Russia’s military logistics network, including operations involving the movement of military equipment between Russian ports and overseas locations. Sparta II was sanctioned by the United States in 2022 over its connections to Oboronlogistika and has been linked to shipments of military equipment from Syria to Russia. The ship has also operated cargo services connecting mainland Russia with its Baltic exclave of Kaliningrad, carrying vehicles, containers and other freight. Despite its military connections, Finnish authorities said they could not confirm whether the vessel was carrying weapons or military equipment when it was attacked. Finland Imposes Air and Maritime Restrictions The drone strike prompted Finland to reintroduce temporary restrictions on aviation and maritime activity in the eastern Gulf of Finland. The Ministry of Defence said the measures were intended to protect civilians and allow authorities to respond to any additional drone threats. Finland also notified its allies of the incident, underscoring the security implications of a military attack taking place near the territorial waters of a NATO member. Finnish authorities said they had received information about Ukrainian drone operations targeting Russia’s Leningrad region earlier Saturday and had taken precautions against drones potentially straying into Finnish territory. Although Finnish officials linked the attack on Sparta II to Ukrainian drones, there was no independently verified confirmation of responsibility from Kyiv in the official statements reviewed. Finland’s Defence Forces said the incident did not represent an immediate military threat to the country and that commercial shipping in the Baltic Sea had not been endangered. War Reaches Another Baltic Shipping Corridor The incident highlights the growing risks to commercial shipping as the war between Russia and Ukraine extends beyond the Black Sea. The Gulf of Finland is one of Russia’s most important maritime corridors, providing access to the Baltic Sea from St. Petersburg and the major oil and cargo terminals at Ust-Luga and Primorsk. It is also a heavily trafficked international shipping route bordered by NATO members Finland and Estonia. Unlike the Black Sea, where merchant vessels have repeatedly been caught up in military operations, the Gulf of Finland has remained a major commercial shipping corridor despite heightened tensions and security concerns since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. The attack on Sparta II raises fresh questions about the vulnerability of Russian military-linked shipping in the Baltic and the potential consequences for neighboring countries when damaged vessels drift across maritime boundaries. It also illustrates the challenges facing coastal authorities when a military incident involving a sanctioned foreign vessel develops into a maritime rescue and potential pollution emergency. The Finnish Border Guard said the situation did not pose a danger to other maritime traffic, while rescue and firefighting operations continued in coordination with other authorities. The fate of Sparta II , including whether the damaged ship can be safely towed back to Russian waters, remains uncertain. REUTERS/Caroline Brehman Nov 21 (Reuters) – The Pacific Maritime Association (PMA) employers group at the Los Angeles and Long Beach ports said on Saturday it had reached a tentative agreement with the union for security guards, averting a strike that could have disrupted operations at the two busiest cargo shipping hubs in the US. The International Longshore and Warehouse Union (ILWU) Local 26 represents 250 security officers, or watchmen, who account for a small fraction of the ports’ workforce, but their work is critical because they control access at terminal gates, conduct security patrols and report safety issues. PMA, which represents terminal owners, said the agreement reached on Saturday was subject to ratification by Local 26 members, and the current contract will be extended pending ratification. The union did not immediately respond to a request for comment sent outside regular business hours. The two sides resumed federally mediated negotiations on Friday, two days after the parties broke off talks , with the employers group reporting “little-to-no movement from the union on PMA’s proposals.” The PMA said at the time that its offer included a one-time bonus of $3,200 for each union member and a wage proposal that would raise average annual earnings for full-time watchmen from more than $170,000 to $198,000. The offer also called for maintaining fully employer-paid healthcare for active workers and retirees, valued at more than $62,000 each year, and increased pension benefits up to $93,200 a year for workers with the longest tenure. Talks between the terminal owners and the union have stretched on for more than a year. (Reporting by Akanksha Khushi in Bengaluru, Steve Gorman and Lisa Baertlein in Los Angeles. articles.summary: More than 110 U.S. trade associations are urging waterfront employers and union leaders to reach a labor agreement and avert a potentially crippling strike at the ports of Los Angeles...
articles.body: Advertise Forum Jobs Subscribe Grab a Seat at the Captain’s Table Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe. Join the leading maritime news network Photo courtesy Port of Long Beach More than 110 U.S. trade associations are urging waterfront employers and union leaders to reach a labor agreement and avert a potentially crippling strike at the ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach, with the latest contract extension set to expire just after midnight Saturday. The warning comes as the Pacific Maritime Association (PMA) and International Longshore and Warehouse Union (ILWU) Local 26 face a critical deadline following more than a year of negotiations over a contract covering approximately 250 port security workers. In a joint statement Friday, the associations called on both sides to remain at the bargaining table, negotiate in good faith and keep cargo moving through the nation’s busiest container port complex. “The Ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach already face congestion from near-record import volumes,” the groups warned, adding that a work stoppage would jeopardize holiday shipments, disrupt manufacturing supply chains and restrict U.S. exports. The statement was backed by major organizations including the National Retail Federation, U.S. Chamber of Commerce, National Association of Manufacturers, American Trucking Associations and more than 100 other groups representing retailers, manufacturers, agricultural producers and logistics providers. The associations warned that a prolonged disruption could quickly spread beyond the waterfront, affecting trucking companies, railroads, warehouses and distribution networks nationwide. Container backlogs could take weeks or months to clear even after operations resume, they said. A Small Union With an Outsized Impact Although Local 26 represents only about 2% of the ILWU workforce at the two ports, its members perform security duties at terminals handling a substantial share of Southern California’s container traffic. According to PMA, the six container terminals covered by the dispute account for approximately 85% of cargo at Long Beach and 33% at Los Angeles. The larger concern is that thousands of longshore workers, marine clerks and foremen covered by separate labor agreements could honor Local 26 picket lines, effectively shutting down cargo operations at affected terminals. PMA warned Wednesday that negotiations held November 17 ended with little progress, while the union had already authorized a strike and indicated it was unwilling to extend the current agreement beyond 12:01 a.m. Pacific time Saturday. The two sides were scheduled to return to the negotiating table Friday in a final effort to avert a work stoppage. The more than 110 trade associations urged both parties to pursue a resolution that protects workers, employers and consumers rather than risk a disruption with nationwide economic consequences. articles.summary: The need for joint European action to strengthen competitiveness, through the effective implementation of the Draghi Report, was highlighted by Greece’s Minister of Maritime Affairs and Insular Policy, Vassilis Kikilias, in a speech following the conference of the European People’s Party (EPP) Group. articles.body: Vassilis Kikilias at the EPP: “We Cannot Afford to Lose Any More Time – Joint European Action Is Needed on Competitiveness and Shipping” in Hellenic Shipping News 21/11/2026 The need for joint European action to strengthen competitiveness, through the effective implementation of the Draghi Report, was highlighted by Greece’s Minister of Maritime Affairs and Insular Policy, Vassilis Kikilias, in a speech following the conference of the European People’s Party (EPP) Group. The conference was held in Athens at the initiative of Eliza Vozemberg, Chair of the European Parliament’s Committee on Transport and Tourism. The Minister stressed that Europe’s strength lies in its elected representatives, who understand the needs of their respective societies, noting that European institutions and administrative bodies must listen to their positions and proposals and take them seriously. “This is the soul and the heart of European politics. Great European leaders in the past contributed to the creation of our European family and the building of the European idea, recognising that people, societies and states must be at the centre of our policies. And, of course, there must be an institutional and administrative framework that implements the policies of the elected representatives of European countries.” He added: “The Draghi Report, approximately two years ago, marked a turning point in addressing the issues we Europeans had been raising concerning competitiveness, the cost of goods and the prosperity of European families. We must be particularly careful and decisive in implementing policies that serve these objectives.” Referring to the strategic importance of shipping to the global economy, the Minister said: “Greece accounts for 61% of the European fleet and 20% of the global fleet, while 80% of world trade is transported by sea. This is an extremely important fact in understanding what is at stake today in Europe and around the world. “Unfortunately, there is a war at the heart of Europe and another in the Middle East. Traffic through the Strait of Hormuz has been disrupted, creating enormous problems for the global economy, as 20% of the world’s oil and 25% of its natural gas pass through it. We are also facing problems with fertiliser supplies. With the war in Ukraine now continuing into its fifth year, we are experiencing even greater difficulties in supply chains, energy and the prices of essential goods. “Therefore, the more we strengthen competitiveness, invest in our ports and shipping, develop our infrastructure and establish an appropriate regulatory framework, the more opportunities we create for growth in our countries, for exporting our products and for prosperity.” As he pointed out, the importance of shipping to national economies and to the everyday lives of European citizens explains Greece’s position on the Net-Zero Framework, both at the IMO and in Europe. “We support the green transition. However, today, liquefied natural gas (LNG) is the transitional fuel, and there is no other available solution, since the quantities of alternative fuels being produced account for just 0.5% of global demand. “We were about to impose an additional financial burden of hundreds of billions of euros on the shipping industry in order to accelerate the green transition using fuels that are not yet available. Had this happened, it would have further fuelled inflation and increased energy and product prices in Europe and across the world. This would have been disastrous for a Europe already under pressure from inflation and facing an energy crisis and a cost-of-living squeeze.” Mr Kikilias went on to discuss the decisive role of ports and their infrastructure in strengthening European competitiveness, stressing: “Our ports are of strategic importance. Why have the United States decided to reinvest in shipyards, shipping, the maritime transportation of energy and ports, and why are China and countries in the East already doing so? Because these sectors will play a decisive role in shaping global power balances and the decisions that will be taken over the next 25 years. “As Europeans, however, we already have this advantage. We have the fleet and we have the ports. This is something we must support. Therefore, when it comes to the Emissions Trading System (ETS), we must take the competitiveness of European ports into account and seek ways to strengthen it, rather than weaken them in comparison with other ports in the Mediterranean or elsewhere in the world.” Concluding his speech, the Minister announced his intention to give shipping a leading role during Greece’s upcoming Presidency of the Council of the European Union, with the participation of representatives of the industry from Greece and across Europe. “As we are due to assume the Presidency of the Council of the European Union in the coming months, I am particularly pleased to announce that we will organise an Informal Meeting of EU Ministers dedicated specifically to shipping. “We will invite the private sector, the President of the Union of Greek Shipowners, Ms Melina Travlou, as well as the leaders of the Greek and European shipping industries, to join you and us – the Members of the European Parliament, members of national parliaments and the Ministry – in meaningful discussions about the future of the sector. “We want to draw on their capabilities so that the many people we represent and support can prosper. This is the way forward, together.” Source: Greek Ministry of Maritime Affairs and Insular Policy 2026-11-21 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.body: Tanker Market: Arabian Gulf Crude Oil Exports Down 27.6% This Year in Hellenic Shipping News 21/11/2026 T he war in Iran has dealt a significant blow to the Gulf oil export markets, with crude oil loading significantly lower over the 10-month period (Jan.-Oct.). In its latest weekly report, shipbroker Banchero Costa said that “in Jan-Dec 2025, global crude oil loadings went up by +1.8% y-o-y to 2,221.1 mln tonnes, excluding all cabotage trade, according to vessels tracking data from LSEG. This year started well, but the trend reversed from March onwards, and global crude oil loadings in Jan-Oct 2026 were down by -5.8% y-o-y to 1,738.8 mln tonnes. Exports from the Arabian Gulf were down by -27.6% y-o-y to 531.3 mln t in Jan-Oct 2026, accounting for 30.6% of seaborne crude trade, down from 39.8% in the same period of last year. From South America, exports increased by +32.5% y-o-y to 238.8 mln t, with a share of 13.7%. Exports from Russian ports (including oil of Kazakh origin) increased by +6.7% y-o-y in Jan-Oct 2026 to 207.8 mln tonnes, or 12.0% of global trade. From the USA, export volumes increased by +8.5% y-o-y to 166.4 mln t in Jan-Oct 2026, a 9.6% share. From South East Asia exports increased by +2.7% y-o-y to 92.8 mln t in Jan-Oct 2026 (but this inevitably also reflects changes in the re-export of Russian origin volumes)”. According to Banchero Costa, “in terms of demand, the top single country seaborne importer of crude oil in Jan-Oct 2026 was Mainland China, accounting for 18.9% of global trade, although the EU27 as a bloc was a larger buyer. Volumes into China declined by -20.1% y-o-y to 328.4 mln t in Jan-Oct 2026. Imports to the EU27 increased by +0.9% y-o-y to 387.8 mln t, accounting for 22.4% of global trade. To ASEAN, imports declined by -9.2% y-o-y to 219.4 mln t (again this includes Russian volumes later reexported elsewhere in Asia). To India, volumes increased +1.5% y-oy to 200.8 mln t in Jan-Oct 2026”. The shipbroker added that “the Arabian Gulf countries (including Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Qatar, Bahrain, Kuwait, Oman, Iraq and Iran) are the single largest seaborne exporter of crude oil in the world. In 2025 they accounted for 39.8% of global seaborne crude oil exports. In the 12 months of 2025, seaborne crude oil exports from AG countries increased by +1.7% to 883.1 mln tonnes, excluding cabotage, after declining by -0.8% y-o-y in 2024. In Jan-Oct 2026, however, Arabian Gulf crude exports collapsed by -27.6% y-o-y to 531.3 mln tonnes, from 734.1 mln t in the same period of 2025, and their share of global seaborne crude trade fell to 30.6%, from 39.8% a year earlier. About 85.8% of volumes loaded in the AG countries in Jan-Oct 2026 were carried in VLCCs, 11.0% were carried in Suezmaxes, and 3.1% in Aframaxes. These proportions increased in recent years in favour of the largest tankers, as Suezmaxes and Afras were diverted to carry more Russian cargoes”. Meanwhile, “the ranking of export terminals has been transformed by the war in the Gulf, with loadings shifting decisively to terminals that can be reached without transiting the Strait of Hormuz. The main crude oil export terminals in the AG are now: Fujairah (137.8 mln tonnes, or 25.9%, in Jan-Oct 2026), Yanbu (104.0 mln t, or 19.6%), Ras Tanura (59.2 mln t, or 11.1%), Basrah (52.6 mln t, or 9.9%), Sohar (49.8 mln t, or 9.4%), Mina al Fahal (36.7 mln t, or 6.9%), Mina al Ahmadi (14.3 mln t), Zirku Island (11.4 mln t), Das Island (6.1 mln t). Ras Tanura, the largest terminal in the world a year ago, has been overtaken by Fujairah and Yanbu, both of which lie outside the Strait”, Banchero Costa said. “In terms of destinations for crude oil shipments from the AG, the focus in recent years has clearly shifted to Asia. In Jan-Oct 2026, the top destination was South East Asia, accounting for 21.6% of the total AG crude exports, narrowly ahead of Mainland China with 21.5%, followed by India with 14.6%, South Korea with 11.0%, Japan with 7.4%. Direct shipments to the USA now account for just 1.8% of AG exports, and direct shipments to the European Union for just 2.2%. Another 6.1% of AG exports are shipped to the Ain Sukhna Terminal in Egypt to feed the Sumed pipeline, and will eventually mostly end up in Europe. In Jan-Oct 2026, the AG countries shipped 114.4 mln tonnes of crude to Mainland China, which represents a -39.4% y-o-y decline from 188.9 mln tonnesin Jan-Oct 2025. Shipments to South East Asia fell by -27.8% y-o-y to 114.9 mln t, from 159.0 mln t in Jan-Oct 2025. The AG also shipped 77.5 mln t this year to India, which represents a decline of -15.4% y-o-y from 91.6 mln t in the same period last year. Volumes to South Korea declined by -28.4% y-o-y in Jan-Oct 2026 to 58.5 mln t. Shipments from the AG to Japan more than halved, down -52.4% y-o-y in JanOct 2026 to 39.4 mln tonnes”, the shipbroker concluded. articles.title: MEPC 85 to confront net-zero divide
articles.summary: The International Maritime Organization’s Marine Environment Protection Committee (MEPC 85) will convene in London from Nov 30-Dec 3 against a backdrop of intensifying pressure to deliver a landmark agreement on shipping decarbonisation, with delegates facing what many observers see as a defining moment for the...
articles.body: MEPC 85 to confront net-zero divide in International Shipping News , Shipping: Emission Possible 21/11/2026 T he International Maritime Organization’s Marine Environment Protection Committee (MEPC 85) will convene in London from Nov 30-Dec 3 against a backdrop of intensifying pressure to deliver a landmark agreement on shipping decarbonisation, with delegates facing what many observers see as a defining moment for the sector’s climate transition. The meeting follows a year of difficult negotiations over the organisation’s proposed mid-term greenhouse gas reduction measures. While the committee’s agenda spans a broad range of environmental issues – including ballast water management, amendments to MARPOL and the NOx Technical Code, marine plastic litter, underwater radiated noise and maritime digitalisation – climate policy is expected to dominate proceedings. Central to those discussions will be efforts to resolve outstanding differences over draft amendments to MARPOL Annex VI and the package of mid-term measures envisioned under the IMO’s 2023 greenhouse gas strategy. According to the IMO, delegates will consider the outcomes of recent intersessional negotiations and seek ways to address “remaining concerns” surrounding the proposed measures, which combine technical and economic elements intended to accelerate emissions reductions from international shipping. The committee is also expected to continue work on the IMO’s Life Cycle GHG Assessment framework. The significance of the discussions has been heightened by the unresolved fate of the IMO’s proposed Net-Zero Framework (NZF), which environmental organisations argue is the industry’s best opportunity to establish a global mechanism for driving down emissions. Adopt ‘as is’ The Clean Shipping Coalition (CSC), representing environmental non-governmental organisations engaged in IMO negotiations, has urged member states to finalise and adopt the framework before the end of the year. “In order to fulfil the goals of the IMO’s GHG Strategy and to protect our global climate, the IMO and all its member states must adopt the Net-Zero Framework ‘as is’, without further diversion,” said Lukas Leppert, president of the Clean Shipping Coalition. “The product of years of negotiations, the Net-Zero Framework reflects findings from the IMO’s Comprehensive Impact Assessment, is a long-negotiated compromise that brings together a multitude of interests and positions, and is supported by a broad majority.” The coalition argues that the framework, originally approved during MEPC 83 in April 2025, already provides a balanced pathway for implementing the IMO’s decarbonisation objectives. The proposed package combines a global fuel standard with an economic mechanism designed to incentivise lower-carbon fuels and technologies. Adoption was delayed after opposition from a group of member states prevented final approval in October 2025. Environmental groups contend that subsequent attempts to replace or significantly revise the framework have failed to attract broad support. “Since October 2025, when IMO member states voted to adjourn the adoption session for one year, various alternative proposals to the NZF were introduced and intensively discussed, but were neither able to demonstrate a comparable reduction in emissions nor gather sufficient support,” Leppert said. “These alternative proposals aimed at supplanting or distracting from the NZF have fallen away, proving the NZF as the best course ahead.” The CSC frames MEPC 85 as a test of the IMO’s ability to convert years of negotiation into binding regulation. “There is no longer time for going in circles; every IMO member state must get behind the Net-Zero Framework and adopt it before the year ends,” Leppert said. EU stance Shipping industry representatives have also taken a view on how member states should proceed. Ahead of the London meetings, Melina Travlos, president of the Union of Greek Shipowners (UGS), warned that political divisions risk undermining efforts to secure a workable global solution. In a statement, she criticised the European Union’s negotiating stance and argued that flexibility remains essential if consensus is to be achieved. “Two months after the inconclusive last round of negotiations at the IMO on reducing greenhouse gas emissions from international shipping, and with the next critical negotiating meetings approaching, there remains no evidence of positive tangible progress,” Travlos said. She argued that recent discussions at European level had demonstrated an unwillingness to compromise, adding that “the EU’s uncompromising position is steering the IMO process to a new dead end, effectively torpedoing the negotiations by depriving them of the flexibility necessary for any chance of success.” The Greek shipowners’ organisation has consistently advocated a global regulatory framework that recognises differing operational realities across shipping segments and trading patterns. Rather than focusing predominantly on alternative fuels, Travlos called for a broader approach incorporating operational and technical efficiency measures. “For a regulation to be effective it must be pragmatic, proportionate and implementable, while reflecting the commercial and operational realities and constraints of the industry,” she said. Travlos further argued that policymakers must align climate ambitions with technological readiness and fuel availability. “This means taking into account the availability, scalability and affordability of alternative fuels, technologies and supporting infrastructure, as well as competing demand from other sectors,” she said. “Such a regulatory framework must also recognise the diversity of solutions available to the shipping industry, rather than focusing exclusively on alternative fuels. It should support all effective pathways to emissions reduction, including technical and operational efficiency measures.” The contrasting positions highlight the challenge awaiting delegates in London. Environmental groups are pressing for rapid adoption of a framework they view as the culmination of years of climate negotiations, while shipowners and several member states are emphasising practicality, flexibility and the risks of imposing measures that outpace technology deployment and fuel availability. After more than a year of delays, MEPC 85 offers member states an opportunity either to bridge their differences and advance a global climate framework or risk prolonging uncertainty over the sector’s pathway to net zero. articles.summary: The price of US sour oil has plunged, as a surge in crude supply from Venezuela, Canada and the Middle East gives refiners ample barrels to choose from.

Join the leading maritime news network Photo: Shutterstock/Sven Hansche By Nathan Risser and Yongchang Chin (Bloomberg) –The price of US sour oil has plunged, as a surge in crude supply from Venezuela, Canada and the Middle East gives refiners ample barrels to choose from. US medium sour export grade Mars traded at a record premium to benchmark West Texas Intermediate futures in the early days of the Iran war. Buyers turned to the Gulf of Mexico variety, which is similar in quality to Middle Eastern crude, as the closure of the Strait of Hormuz disrupted supplies. Now, as oil markets begin to settle after a volatile year, Mars has fallen to a deep discount, making it cheaper for US refiners built to process heavier crude. Mars has dropped from a $10 premium to a $4 discount to WTI futures in less than a month. That’s the steepest discount since late September. Mars rallied to record premium of $17.50 at the peak of supply disruptions in March and April. At the start of the year, before the US and Israel launched their war in Iran in late February, the grade largely traded at a discount. Rising production of heavy-sour crude in Venezuela and Canada has pushed global prices lower in recent weeks. US refiners, major buyers of heavier oil along the Gulf Coast and in the Midwest, have benefited from increased supplies from Canada and Latin America. At the same time, higher shipping costs are weighing on prices at the barrel’s origin by making overseas sales more expensive. Flows from the Persian Gulf have also increased. Higher Middle Eastern flows, however, have reduced the incentive for Asian refiners to take advantage of falling Mars prices, with the US grade still uneconomical to import, according to traders familiar with the matter, who asked not to be named because they aren’t authorized to speak to the media. On a delivered basis to Northeast Asia, Mars for February was priced at a premium of about $12 to $13 a barrel to the Dubai benchmark — around $10 more expensive than similar quality oil from Saudi Arabia, they said. At least one other seller of Middle Eastern crude has also slashed offer prices, they added. “Incremental supply looks to be dominated by heavier and more sour barrels, especially out of Canada, Venezuela, and the Middle East,” Valero’s head of crude supply Randy Hawkins said in an October earnings call. It’s a “race to the bottom” Phillips 66’s executive vice president of marketing and commercial Brian Mandell said on a call with analysts the same month. In Canada, the pipeline that takes oil sands crude from inland fields to export markets on the West Coast is operating at a record 960,000 barrels a day this month, 8% above its stated capacity. Oil will also be shipped on 34 vessels out of the Westridge terminal near Vancouver in November, up from 31 in October. While cheaper heavy crude is a boon to refiners who are already making record profits from the Iran war’s disruptions to global fuel markets, it is coming at a cost to heavy oil producers. “We’re basically going to have to be a price taker,” oil driller Sable Offshore Corp. chief executive office Jim Flores said earlier this month. Sable pumps heavy oil off the coast of California. For now, US crude exports of both heavy and light grades continue at historically elevated levels. US crude exports averaged 4 million barrels a day over the past four weeks, below the weekly record of more than 6 million set in April but well above the 3 million average since the US lifted its crude-export ban in 2015. © 2026 Bloomberg L.P. November 20, 2026 © Adobe Stock/IbrahimAlkan A tanker caught fire after being struck by an unknown projectile while sailing outbound through the Strait of Hormuz, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency said on Friday. The British navy-affiliated agency UKMTO said that the incident occurred 8 nautical miles north of the Omani town of Khasab, adding that no casualties or environmental impact were reported. Iran's Revolutionary Guards said shortly afterwards that an oil tanker had caught fire after hitting a mine while attempting to transit the Strait of Hormuz near Khasab, Iranian state media reported. November 20, 2026 © Adobe Stock/christianthiel.net US Treasury Department officials met with government authorities in Singapore and Malaysia this week, including regulators and national security bodies, to warn of potential risks they could face if they do not comply with US sanctions on Iran. Washington is urging the countries, as well as law firms and banks operating there, to stay alert for Iranian front companies, as it steps up efforts to enforce sanctions in Asia and bring about a speedy end to the conflict in the Middle East. The US is urging additional scrutiny on "high-risk" sectors such as maritime transport, aviation services and procurement networks, "to make sure they're not fronting for Iran," said a Treasury Department official. "We want it to be understood too, that we're going to target these lifelines, and it's not going to be a negotiation when we find a lifeline that needs to be targeted," the official said. Since the US and Israel commenced strikes on Iran in February, the US has intensified actions to throttle Tehran's business interests overseas. In August, President Donald Trump's administration launched Operation Economic Outcast, resulting in a barrage of sanctions against targets spanning Canadian digital currency platforms to a major Russian banking group. OIL ON WATER For years, tankers have regularly made stops in the waters around Malaysia, Singapore and Indonesia to make ship-to-ship transfers of Iranian oil that help obscure its origin. Last year, Malaysian authorities said they would more tightly enforce rules around these transfers and in February seized two tankers and their cargoes. Since April, the US Navy has imposed a blockade on shipping reaching Iran through the Strait of Hormuz, and this month has cracked down on movement over Iran's land borders and through the Caspian Sea. In July, the Treasury Department sanctioned dozens of individuals, vessels and companies based in Singapore, Hong Kong, the UAE, the Marshall Islands and St Kitts and Nevis linked to Iranian oil magnate Mohammad Hossein Shamkhani. These efforts were starting to disrupt Iran's source of revenue, the US official said, citing data showing that the country is currently undergoing the worst GDP contraction in four decades and the highest rate of inflation since World War II. IRANIAN AIRLINES However, the official said there was still work to be done. "There's an Iranian airline that flies to Malaysia, or has, recently, so we raised this," the US official said, without naming the carrier. Using public flight records, Reuters identified a regularly scheduled flight between Tehran and Kuala Lumpur operated by Iran Airtour, which flew as recently as November 14. A scheduled flight on November 17 did not depart, the records also show. Iran Airtour did not respond to an emailed request for comment sent outside of business hours on Friday. Most Iranian airlines largely stopped flying to Malaysia in 2022 due to US sanctions on refuelling Iranian planes. However, Iran Airtour, a privately owned airline, resumed flights to Malaysia in November 2025, according to Iranian media. On September 8, the US imposed sanctions on dozens of companies in the UAE, Britain, Malaysia, Turkey and Kazakhstan it said were supporting Iran's aviation sector to move weapons, personnel and illicit cargo. The following day, Iran Air officials met with Malaysia's ambassador to Iran to discuss resuming direct flights between Iran and Kuala Lumpur. 'DOING OUR PART' Both Malaysia and Singapore implement UN Security Council sanctions on Iran. Singapore's government said in a statement it "is firmly committed to doing our part" and "preventing bad actors from abusing our corporate vehicles," citing its efforts to strengthen vigilance in the maritime and financial industries this year. The Malaysian government did not respond to requests for comment. (Reuters)

articles.body: Saudi Forces Strike Hodeidah Port as Houthis Warn Airlines Away From Airspace Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 20, 2026 © AU USAnakul / Adobe Stock The Saudi-led coalition fighting Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis said it had struck the Red Sea port of Hodeidah to destroy Houthi capabilities on Friday, as the militants warned airlines to avoid Saudi airspace, pledging new air strikes within hours. The developments, a day after the group struck the tallest skyscraper in Riyadh, signalled a worsening of a conflict that has brought a humanitarian crisis to Yemen and severe disruption to Saudi Arabia, in parallel with the US-led war against Iran. Hodeidah is the main port bringing food and other supplies into Houthi-controlled northern Yemen. The coalition had earlier warned civilians to evacuate the area. The Saudi-led coalition said it destroyed operational capabilities at the port that were used in smuggling operations and the transport of weapons and ballistic missiles. The port remains fully operational and the flow of goods will continue, according to Yemen’s Information Minister. HOUTHIS TELL SHIPPING COMPANIES TO EVACUATE FROM SAUDI PORTS There was no immediate comment from the Houthis, who had earlier said they would hit Red Sea ports if the Saudis carried out their own threat to strike the Yemeni port. "We warn all employees, workers, and those in the vicinity of (Saudi Arabia's Red Sea) ports to evacuate them immediately and stay away. We also urge all shipping companies to immediately evacuate their ships from these ports," Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said in a statement. Airlines should avoid Saudi airspace "because it will be the scene of our operations in the coming hours," Saree said, making an exception for airspace near the Muslim holy cities of Mecca and Medina. He also said the group would target a power station at Shuqaiq in southern Saudi Arabia. The Saudi-led coalition also said it carried out an operation in Yemen's capital Sanaa targeting ballistic missile and drone capabilities and that operations in Saada and Taiz were ongoing. Since fighting resumed in Yemen in July in parallel with the wider Iran war, the Houthis have rapidly advanced in Yemen, seizing territory from Yemen's internationally recognised government and its allies, who are backed by Saudi Arabia. The Saudis have carried out air strikes on Yemen in support of their allies on the ground, while the Houthis have struck Saudi oil targets, airports and office towers. Deadly strikes on Riyadh's main airport last month led to the cancellation of most international flights, and Saudi Arabia has postponed or cancelled high-profile global events including soccer's AFC Asian Cup. Saudi Arabia, a close ally of the United States, has been backing Yemen's internationally recognised government for more than a decade in a war that was fought to a stalemate in 2022 but reignited in July this year. REUTERS/Stringer Another tanker was struck by a projectile and caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz on Friday, extending a wave of attacks on commercial shipping that has pushed maritime security incidents to their highest weekly level since mid-October. The latest incident occurred at approximately 1500 UTC, eight nautical miles north of Khasab, Oman, according to UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) Warning 214-26 . The tanker was transiting outbound through the strategic waterway when an unknown projectile struck its port bow, sparking a fire onboard. The vessel’s company security officer reported no casualties or environmental impact. Authorities are investigating. The attack comes amid a sharp escalation in threats to merchant shipping across the Middle East and Black Sea. According to maritime security analyst Martin Kelly of Orbital Risk Intelligence, shipping experienced 15 attacks and piracy-related incidents over the past seven days, a 50% increase from the previous week and the highest weekly total since mid-October. In the Persian Gulf, Strait of Hormuz and Gulf of Oman, Kelly recorded seven strikes involving six vessels. Four tankers were hit within 13 nautical miles of Khasab over three days, including the LPG tanker TARA GAS , which was attacked twice. The violence has left two seafarers missing and 13 injured, according to Kelly’s assessment. Among the most serious incidents was the November 17 attack on the tanker NAVIG8 MESSI , which suffered a fire after being struck 13 nautical miles north of Khasab. ADNOC confirmed that one crew member was missing and 11 others were injured. The remaining crew were evacuated and the vessel was reported under tow. The TARA GAS , meanwhile, was disabled by a projectile strike on November 16 before being hit again the following day, resulting in another fire and the vessel being abandoned. The pattern points to an increasingly dangerous concentration of attacks along the southern shipping lanes off Oman’s Musandam Peninsula, particularly against tankers attempting to leave the Persian Gulf. The deteriorating security situation is taking a continued toll on commercial traffic. In its weekly maritime security overview published Friday , UKMTO reported 115 outbound and 148 inbound transits over the preceding seven days, down from 139 outbound and 169 inbound crossings the previous week. Combined traffic remains approximately 65% below pre-conflict levels. UKMTO recorded six verified attacks across the Strait of Hormuz and Persian Gulf during its latest reporting period, which covered incidents through November 18. Four occurred in the Strait itself and two in the wider Persian Gulf. Two vessels required assistance, while the outcomes of four others remained unknown. The agency cautioned that its figures do not capture every incident, as some reports cannot be independently verified. Since the U.S.-Iran ceasefire agreement expired on August 17, UKMTO has recorded six total vessel losses, while 22 vessels required assistance and 31 were confirmed to have continued their voyages. The Joint Maritime Information Center (JMIC) continues to assess the threat to commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz as SEVERE , warning that further deliberate attacks are highly likely. The surge in maritime violence extends well beyond the Middle East. Six commercial vessels were struck in the western Black Sea over the past week, according to Kelly, including two ships that sank in Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone on consecutive days. The general cargo ship BETUL 8 sank on November 16, followed by the LPG tanker GAS HUSKY on November 17. All 31 seafarers aboard the two vessels were rescued. Maritime security firm Ambrey separately confirmed reports of six vessels struck since November 13, including four attacked near the Sulina anchorage in Romanian waters and two in Bulgarian waters. Ambrey assessed the attacks as part of an escalating Russian campaign involving unmanned aerial and surface vessels. The incidents have raised growing concerns about the safety of commercial shipping in waters adjacent to NATO member states Romania and Bulgaria. Piracy-related activity has also increased in the Gulf of Aden and western Indian Ocean. During the week, a tanker reported being approached by an armed skiff carrying a ladder approximately 430 nautical miles east of Socotra, Yemen. In another incident off Al Mukalla, armed guards aboard a cargo vessel fired a warning shot to repel an attempted boarding. A further incident was reported Friday, when six armed men aboard a skiff fired four shots at an eastbound bulk carrier approximately 95 nautical miles southwest of Al Mukalla. The ship’s security team returned warning shots, forcing the attackers to retreat. No injuries or damage were reported. The incidents underscore the growing range of threats facing merchant vessels, from projectile and drone attacks in active conflict zones to renewed piracy activity along established trading routes. With attacks concentrated around the Strait of Hormuz and the western Black Sea, maritime security analysts warn that the coming week could bring further strikes against commercial vessels. November 20, 2026 © Dongara Marine The Cook Labor Government is investing $13.4 million in two new vessels to strengthen fisheries compliance and protect the Kimberley's valuable marine resources. A new nine-meter amphibious vessel is now operating out of Broome, undertaking patrols across the Buccaneer Archipelago Marine Park. The vessel was built by global business Sealegs who specialize in manufacturing the versatile craft. The vessel's ability to travel on both land and water will allow Fisheries and Marine Officers to access remote locations where extreme tidal conditions and limited boat ramp infrastructure can make launching traditional vessels difficult. The vessel will support joint patrols with local Aboriginal ranger groups, strengthening partnerships and supporting the shared management of the culturally significant region. Expected to be delivered in October 2028, the new vessel will be built by Dongara Marine, providing another boost to Western Australia's marine manufacturing industry. November 20, 2026 © Hatenboer-Water Hatenboer-Water has started building a new headquarters in Schiedam, driving the first foundation pile on Thursday after early demolition work. Due to finish in the third quarter of 2027, the new building project adds manufacturing space and twice the company's current testing capacity as orders grow across shipping and offshore energy. Hatenboer-Water's existing premises in Schiedam have reached their limit. Rebuilding on site upgrades its engineering workshops and manufacturing facilities and keeps the business inside the Port of Rotterdam maritime cluster. Schiedam's focus on maritime manufacturing puts the company close to European shipbuilders, engineering firms and offshore service providers. The site also serves as the main hub for regional offices in Aberdeen, Dubai, Houston, Singapore and Hamburg. Doubling production and testing capacity means Hatenboer-Water can build more systems and run several demanding tests simultaneously, cutting waiting times and speeding up delivery. Inside, the building includes new production equipment, a better layout for moving materials, shared meeting spaces for visiting clients, and upgraded IT infrastructure and access controls. Separate, fully secured office zones with restricted access will let teams work on confidential projects. Designed as an all-electric, fully insulated building, it will also operate without natural gas. Daily operations will not stop during construction. Using a phased 'chessboard' plan, the existing building will stay in use while the first new sections are built. Staff and equipment will move across step by step as each part finishes, keeping production and support running as normal through 2027.

Azule Energy has completed the sale of its participating interests in blocks 14 and 14K offshore Angola to Etu Energias. The transaction comprises 20% participating interest in Block 14 and 10% participating interest in Block 14K, with the completion following the fulfilment of the applicable conditions and receipt of the required approvals. The company explains that this transaction supports the continued optimization of its portfolio and focus on strategic priorities, while reinforcing its long-term commitment to the country and its energy sector. Rand Merchant Bank (RMB), a division of FirstRand Bank, served as the sole financial advisor to Azule Energy on the transaction. " The completion of this transaction is another important step in the continued optimisation of Azule Energy’s portfolio. It enables us to focus our investment and capabilities on our strategic priorities while maintaining our long-term commitment to Angola and its energy sector. We would like to thank our partners, RMB, the relevant authorities and all those involved in supporting a safe and orderly transition. articles.body: Vice Adm. Burdian appointed as DHS Joint Task Force-Maritime Director Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 20, 2026 Vice Adm. Jo‑Ann Burdian. Image courtesy USCG Vice Adm. Jo‑Ann Burdian was presidentially appointed as the director, Department of Homeland Security Joint Task Force–Maritime (JTF-M), effective Nov. 10, 2026. DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin nominated Burdian as director of JTF-M, in accordance with 6 U.S.C. § 348(b)(3)(A), to ensure the critical, continued role of JTF-M in synchronizing multi-agency maritime operations and securing the nation’s maritime borders. “Vice Admiral Burdian’s appointment as the JTF-M director marks a pivotal moment for our collective maritime defense," said Mullin. "Her unmatched operational expertise is critical as JTF-M continues to dismantle illicit networks, prevent hostile exploitation of our maritime borders, and leverage the MOC-P construct to achieve departmental unity of effort and drive nationwide success." JTF-M synchronizes DHS component operations, intelligence, and investigations across the maritime domain to secure U.S. borders, prevent and respond to homeland security crises and facilitate regionally based joint operations. As the DHS Maritime Operations Coordination Plan (MOC-P) program office, JTF-M enhances coordination among DHS components, eliminating redundancy and increasing effectiveness through 35 Regional Coordinating Mechanisms (ReCoMs). These ReCoMs execute DHS missions at every major U.S. port, along all U.S. coastlines and approaches to maritime borders of the U.S. and its territories. The ReCoMs help prevent terrorist, criminal, and hostile activities and dismantle illicit networks attempting to exploit the maritime domain and reduce vulnerabilities while safeguarding legal trade and travel. "I am honored to lead the dedicated staff of Joint Task Force-Maritime as we strengthen our borders and streamline interagency response," said Burdian. "Through our 35 ReCoMs and strong partnerships with the Department of War, we will continue to safeguard legal trade and travel while remaining an impenetrable barrier against cross-border smuggling, illegal immigration and illicit trafficking." Burdian also serves as commander, Coast Guard Atlantic Area and commander, Coast Guard Defense Force East, providing Coast Guard forces and operations across all mission areas from the Arctic Ocean to the Arabian Gulf in support of the DoW and combatant commanders for national defense missions.
